items.title: Getting news on gaming platforms like Discord and Twitch is linked to more radical political views
items.summary:
Young Europeans who get their news from gaming platforms like Discord, Steam, or Twitch tend to hold stronger radical political views than peers who rely on social media or traditional news, according to research published in Political Psychology .

A similar pattern appeared among youth who get news through private messaging apps like Telegram and WhatsApp. Simply playing video games or using these spaces for everyday socializing, however, was not linked to higher radical beliefs.

Why closed online spaces draw scrutiny 
 Online political talk has increasingly moved from public feeds like Facebook and X into closed spaces, including private messaging apps and gaming-adjacent platforms where players coordinate matches, join private servers, and watch livestreamers. Researchers studying youth extremism are examining how getting news in these spaces relates to radical belief dispositions, a cluster of attitudes spanning conspiracy thinking, authoritarianism, prejudice against minority groups, traditional masculinity, and openness to political violence.

Earlier work has documented how extremist actors target online leisure communities. In a 2024 systematic review of research on right-wing extremism in video games , scholars summarized evidence indicating that far-right groups use hate speech and ideological themes in gaming spaces as an on-ramp to recruit disillusioned players. Meanwhile, a 2022 series of three studies found that players whose personal identities fuse tightly with gamer culture tend to endorse more racism, sexism, and extreme behavior, especially when lonely…
items.t: Getting news on gaming platforms like Discord and Twitch is linked to more radical political views

items.title: Disadvantaged students with a growth mindset are more likely to beat the odds, especially when their peers share it
items.summary:
An analysis of data from more than 600,000 15-year-olds in 79 countries found that socioeconomically disadvantaged students with a growth mindset were more likely to be academically resilient, meaning they reached solid levels of proficiency in reading, math, and science despite their backgrounds. Resilience was most common among students with a growth mindset who also attended schools where their peers tended to hold growth mindsets. The paper was published in npj Science of Learning .

Students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds tend to face substantial obstacles to academic success. Yet some manage to perform well despite these challenges, an ability known as academic resilience. Researchers have identified various individual and environmental factors that potentially contribute to academic resilience, including students’ confidence, engagement, and academic expectations, as well as a safe and orderly school environment and good teaching.

One potentially important factor is a growth mindset, the belief that intelligence and abilities can be developed through effort and effective learning strategies, rather than being fixed and unchangeable. Students with a growth mindset tend to demonstrate greater perseverance, more adaptive responses to failure, and a stronger willingness to embrace challenges. However, previous research has produced mixed findings about its relationship with academic achievement among disadvantaged students.

Recent research also suggests that the benefits of a growth mindset may depend on the social environment, particularly the…

items.title: Traits that make someone seem more intellectual can also make them seem less liberal, study suggests
items.summary:
People’s impressions of how politically liberal and how intellectual another person is do not behave like two expressions of a single broad personality trait, according to new experimental research published in Journal of Research in Personality . When participants evaluated fictional individuals from brief personality profiles, descriptions that boosted perceived intellect tended to lower perceived liberalism. The findings suggest that combining political attitudes and intellectual curiosity into one broad “openness to experience” score may obscure distinct underlying dimensions in how people judge others.

In psychology, personality is commonly organized around the Big Five model, which groups traits into five broad domains: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness to experience. Openness to experience refers to a person’s tendency to engage with new ideas, art, emotions, and unconventional values.

Widely used personality questionnaires calculate a single overall openness score by adding together six narrower sub-traits, called facets. Two of those facets are intellect, which captures an interest in abstract or philosophical ideas, and liberalism, which reflects progressive political views and a willingness to question traditional rules or authority.

Psychologists have debated whether these varied facets belong on a single psychological spectrum. In a 2007 study , researchers identified two distinct aspects within openness: an intellect aspect centered on reasoning and abstract thought, and an openness aspect centered on aesthetics,…
items.t: Traits that make someone seem more intellectual can also make them seem less liberal, study suggests

items.title: Moral anger overrides credibility and accelerates the spread of misinformation online
items.summary:
When people feel moral anger, they become more likely to share false information online and pay less attention to the credibility of the source. This emotional reaction lowers the cognitive threshold required to make a sharing decision, leading to faster and more impulsive social media habits. The findings were published in the journal Cognition and Emotion .

Social media platforms are saturated with morally charged content. Often, this content is designed to evoke moral outrage to maximize user engagement. Moral outrage is a broad emotional response to perceived injustices or violations of social norms. It typically consists of two distinct emotions: moral anger and moral disgust. 

Psychological theories propose that these two emotions motivate different types of behavior. Moral anger generally encourages approach-oriented actions, such as confronting a wrongdoer, demanding punishment, or raising awareness about an injustice. Moral disgust usually prompts avoidance behaviors, such as distancing oneself from an offending person or attempting to isolate a social contaminant. 

Despite the prevalence of moral outrage on the internet, the specific roles of anger and disgust in spreading information have remained somewhat ambiguous. Psychologists Haoyang Jiang and Hongbo Yu, along with their colleagues at Shenzhen University and the University of California Santa Barbara, wanted to understand how these distinct emotions influence behavior. Specifically, they investigated how moral anger and moral disgust affect a person’s willingness to share misinformation.

When people…

items.title: Breathwork can induce altered states comparable to moderate psychedelic doses, study finds
items.summary:
Mental health professionals who participated in a structured session of rapid, continuous breathing reported psychedelic-like shifts in consciousness and rated the practice’s clinical potential well above its risks, according to a new exploratory study published in npj Mental Health Research . While the clinicians saw promise for conditions such as depression and anxiety, they advised caution for severe psychiatric disorders and emphasized that firsthand enthusiasm does not establish whether the technique works as a medical treatment.

High ventilation breathwork refers to practices that involve prolonged, deliberate hyperventilation, typically performed for 30 minutes to several hours while lying down in a group setting with trained facilitators and emotionally evocative music. Unlike slow-paced breathing exercises aimed at simple relaxation, sustained fast and deep breathing lowers carbon dioxide levels in the blood and shifts blood acidity, triggering physical sensations such as tingling or muscle tightness alongside changes in brain blood flow and nervous system activity.

Scientific interest in these breathing practices has grown alongside psychedelic-assisted therapy, as substances like LSD and psilocybin can evoke intense shifts in perception and emotion but face strict legal regulations, high costs, and medical safety constraints. In a 2023 review , researchers outlined how rapid breathing modulates brain chemistry and bodily awareness, proposing that it could eventually serve as a non-drug tool in psychiatric care.

Building on that idea, a 2025 study led by…
items.t: Breathwork can induce altered states comparable to moderate psychedelic doses, study finds

items.title: Mothers in larger families show less tolerance for young children’s anger
items.summary:
Mothers raising multiple children tend to be less tolerant of a young child’s expressions of anger compared to mothers raising fewer children. This lowered acceptance of aggressive emotional displays occurs regardless of the mother’s general parenting stress or mindfulness levels. The research was published in Cognition and Emotion .

Parents help children learn which emotional responses are acceptable through a process known as emotion socialization. A parent’s beliefs about childrearing dictate how they respond to a crying toddler or a frustrated preschooler. These responses teach children how to regulate and express their feelings in social situations. The early childhood years, generally spanning ages two to six, represent a period of rapid development in a child’s ability to understand and manage emotions.

Early childhood is an important developmental window where toddlers transition into school-aged children. During this period, children experience neurological changes that support basic emotion regulation. Parents adjust their expectations as children grow, often holding older preschoolers to a higher standard of behavioral control than toddlers. Exploring this specific age range allows researchers to capture a dynamic phase of parenting.

Psychologists often divide negative emotions into two categories based on how they affect social interactions. Dominant negative emotions, such as anger and frustration, are typically viewed as more disruptive to a household. Submissive negative emotions, like sadness and fear, are often met with more supportive or comforting…
items.t: Mothers in larger families show less tolerance for young children’s anger

items.title: Low-dose THC makes people feel high without relieving distress from stressful memories
items.summary:
Low oral doses of THC, the main intoxicating compound in cannabis, did not ease emotional distress or bodily stress reactions when healthy young adults were reminded of a stressful social experience, according to new research published in Psychopharmacology . Although the drug made participants feel noticeably high and appeared to quiet a pattern of nervous smiling during the memory reminders, it left their feelings of distress unchanged both during the session and a week later. The findings suggest that while many people use cannabis hoping to take the edge off difficult memories, modest doses of THC may not dull the emotional sting of recalling a stressful event.

Cannabis use has grown increasingly common among young adults in the United States, and relief from stress or troubling memories is among the reasons users cite most often. Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, known as THC, acts on the body’s endocannabinoid system, a network of chemical signals and cellular receptors concentrated in brain regions that regulate mood, fear, and stress. When someone encounters sights or sounds tied to a past stressful episode, those reminders can reactivate the memory and trigger renewed feelings of tension and discomfort.

Interest in using cannabinoids to soften stressful memories grew out of earlier discoveries about how the endocannabinoid system handles fear and real-time stress. In a 2002 animal study , scientists found that the brain’s natural cannabinoid signaling is needed to gradually extinguish learned fear responses to aversive memories. Later human research pointed to…
items.t: Low-dose THC makes people feel high without relieving distress from stressful memories

items.title: Massive field experiment suggests classroom phone bans modestly improve college grades
items.summary:
Requiring college students to store their smartphones in wooden boxes during lectures tends to produce modest improvements in academic performance, according to a large-scale field experiment published in Science . The gains were concentrated among lower-performing students and first-year undergraduates, and students who experienced the classroom rule generally became more supportive of phone restrictions by the end of the semester.

Classroom smartphone bans are policies that require students to hand over or store away their mobile devices during instructional time rather than keeping them at their desks. Education systems around the world have increasingly adopted these rules in primary and secondary schools to reduce distraction, curb digital addiction, and limit cyberbullying. In the United States, citing a 2023 education policy report, the authors note that roughly two-thirds of states had enacted some form of phone legislation, with remaining states considering similar measures.

Despite this rapid policy shift, large-scale experimental evidence on how classroom phone restrictions affect learning, well-being, and daily behavior has remained scarce. Past observational and quasi-experimental studies have produced mixed results, ranging from academic or well-being improvements among struggling students to little measurable change, while research on classroom laptops indicates that unrestricted device access can impair learning.

Studies conducted across different settings also illustrate how complex the relationship between smartphones and student outcomes can be. For…
items.t: Massive field experiment suggests classroom phone bans modestly improve college grades

items.title: How brain cell networks expand and shrink as cocaine habits form
items.summary:
As mice learn to self-administer cocaine, the cluster of brain cells driving this behavior initially expands before shrinking back down as the habit solidifies. This discovery reveals that the brain networks managing addiction are constantly swapping out individual cells even when outward actions remain stable. The findings were published in a small study in The Journal of Neuroscience .

Developing a substance use disorder typically follows a predictable sequence of behavioral changes. It starts with an initial learning phase to acquire the drug, followed by a period where the drug-taking routine stabilizes, and finally a maintenance phase where the habit becomes automatic.

Researchers wanted to understand exactly what happens inside the brain’s cellular circuitry during these behavioral transitions. To answer this question, investigators focused on a small, deep-brain structure called the nucleus accumbens. This region acts as a major hub for processing motivation, rewards, and physical movement.

Most of the cells in this area are called medium spiny neurons. These neurons receive signals from various parts of the brain and act like gates. They decide whether an animal should take a specific action to get a reward.

A team of scientists led by neuroscientists Linjie Jin, Xiguang Qi, and Yan Dong at the University of Pittsburgh designed an experiment to watch these cells in real time. They aimed to map how the network adapts while an animal actively learns to seek out cocaine over an extended period.

The research team trained male mice to self-administer cocaine by…
items.t: How brain cell networks expand and shrink as cocaine habits form

items.title: New study finds bosses who share stories about their own good deeds risk disgusting employees
items.summary:
When managers tell employees about their own ethical actions at work, those stories can inspire workers to be more helpful, or they can come across as distasteful bragging. New research published in Journal of Applied Psychology suggests that whether a boss’s moral stories uplift or alienate employees depends in part on whether that manager also highlights the good deeds of others.

In organizational psychology, telling colleagues about positive events one has experienced on the job is known as workplace capitalization. Typical examples include mentioning a promotion, a pay raise, a met goal, or a successful project.

Past research indicates that when supervisors talk up their own professional accomplishments, employees tend to view them as more competent, though often less warm and likable. Even well-meaning positivity from a boss can carry hidden costs within workplace hierarchies. For example, a 2026 study of workplace leaders and subordinates found that when managers share personal good news, employees often feel pressured to put on an enthusiastic display, leaving them emotionally drained and less inclined to help out coworkers.

Less was known about what happens when bosses spotlight ethical conduct rather than career achievements. Co-first authors Grace Ching Chi Ho , an assistant professor of management at Southern Methodist University’s Cox School of Business, and Hudson Sessions, an associate professor in the Department of Management and Entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W. P. Carey School of Business, examined what they call supervisor moral…
items.t: New study finds bosses who share stories about their own good deeds risk disgusting employees

items.title: College students who spend more time in intense physical activity report slightly fewer depressive symptoms
items.summary:
A survey of more than 2,600 students at the University of Milan in Italy found that those who reported spending more of their waking time in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity tended to report slightly fewer depressive symptoms and slightly better health. Those who reported spending more time sitting tended to report slightly more depressive symptoms and slightly worse health. The paper was published in Depression and Anxiety .

University students often experience substantial psychological distress. A recent review of studies conducted in Italy estimated that 46% of university students experienced depressive symptoms, 65% experienced anxiety symptoms, and 85% experienced significant stress, although estimates varied considerably across studies and some were conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Many university students engage in very little physical activity and spend prolonged periods sitting, both of which may be associated with poorer mental and physical health. However, time spent on different activities is interconnected, because increasing time devoted to one activity necessarily reduces the time available for others. For example, spending an additional 15 minutes exercising means spending 15 fewer minutes sitting or doing something else.

Study author Flavia Pennisi and colleagues examined how the balance of time university students spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, light physical activity, and sedentary behavior during their waking hours was associated with their depressive symptoms, self-rated health, and eating disorder symptoms. They also…
items.t: College students who spend more time in intense physical activity report slightly fewer depressive symptoms

items.title: Parents who spank are more likely to hit a child out of anger years later, study finds
items.summary:
A national study of American parents indicates that at age 35, routine disciplinary spanking and hitting a child out of anger are linked to largely different personal and household characteristics. In an overlapping sample followed over five years, parents who spanked at age 35 had over twice the odds of losing their temper and hitting or throwing things at their children at age 40. Published in Family Process , the findings suggest everyday spanking and anger-driven hitting may have distinct roots even as milder discipline predicts harsher aggression later on.

Corporal punishment refers to using physical force to correct or control a child’s behavior, from open-handed spanking on the buttocks to washing a mouth out with soap or hitting with an object. Over one in three U.S. parents use physical discipline, despite opposition from groups like the American Academy of Pediatrics citing harm to children. Although some analyses argue mild, infrequent spanking has minimal negative effects, harsher forms can cross into physical abuse.

Studying physical discipline is complicated because surveys often group very different behaviors together. Prior work links physical punishment to personal history, beliefs, mental health, and stress; for instance, an earlier study of parents found that adults with difficult childhoods, especially those spanked growing up, were over twice as likely to spank their own children. Yet routine discipline and harsher aggression can have different predictors. In a 2019 study of 310 Black parents , higher income within a low-income sample predicted less…
items.t: Parents who spank are more likely to hit a child out of anger years later, study finds

items.title: People judge larger bodies as more forgiving, study suggests
items.summary:
A recent study found that people in China tend to view individuals with larger bodies as more forgiving than those with thinner bodies. This perception seems to stem from a tendency to judge heavier individuals as warmer and more approachable. The research was published in the British Journal of Psychology .

When humans form first impressions, they rely heavily on visual cues to guess a stranger’s moral character. Psychologists often use a framework called the Stereotype Content Model to understand these rapid judgments. This model suggests that people evaluate strangers along two main dimensions: warmth, which involves kindness and trustworthiness, and competence, which involves intelligence and confidence.

Past studies have shown that observers frequently stereotype heavier individuals as warmer but less competent than thinner individuals. Observers also rely on mental shortcuts to assume that if someone possesses one trait, they naturally possess related characteristics. Because the concept of forgivingness overlaps with warmth, an observer might automatically assume a warm-seeming person is also quick to pardon an offense.

Past research has mostly examined what makes a person actually forgiving, linking the trait to personality factors like agreeableness. Less is understood about how observers decide if someone else is forgiving just by looking at them. In Chinese culture, linguistic idioms directly connect a larger physical size to an accommodating nature. One phrase translates to having a broad mind and a fat body, while another uses a large belly as a metaphor…
items.t: People judge larger bodies as more forgiving, study suggests

items.title: Even when calories and nutrients match, ultraprocessed foods trigger a larger insulin surge
items.summary:
Eating an ultraprocessed meal triggers a substantially higher surge in blood insulin, slightly higher post-meal calorie burning, and a slower shift toward burning carbohydrates compared to a non-ultraprocessed meal with nearly identical nutrients, according to a clinical trial published in Nature Metabolism .

These post-meal metabolic shifts also tracked with how reward-processing areas of the brain reacted to photographs of food, even though volunteers reported liking both types of food equally and bid similar amounts of money for them. Together, the findings indicate that industrial food processing alters how the body and brain respond to a meal through pathways that go beyond calories, fat, sugar, or fiber alone.

From nutrient counts to gut-to-brain reward signals 
 Under the Nova classification system, which groups foods by the extent and purpose of industrial processing, ultraprocessed foods are factory-manufactured formulations created through multiple physical and chemical transformations. Common manufacturing steps include breaking whole crops down into isolated starches, oils, and proteins, heating ingredients under high pressure through extrusion, and adding flavorings, emulsifiers, or colorings rarely used in home kitchens.

Products in this category account for 55 percent of the calories consumed in the United States, according to federal dietary survey data. Large population studies link heavy intake to obesity, metabolic disease, and cancer, though skeptics argue those risks simply reflect excess calories, fat, and sugar rather than processing itself.…
items.t: Even when calories and nutrients match, ultraprocessed foods trigger a larger insulin surge

items.title: Evolutionary hypothesis linking facial symmetry to women’s mating behavior fails to hold up in new study
items.summary:
Women with more symmetrical faces are no more open to casual sex or more sexually active than women with less symmetrical faces once their living environment and relationship status are taken into account, according to a new study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior . Initial comparisons among Polish women hinted at a slight connection between facial symmetry and certain sexual attitudes and behaviors, but that pattern disappeared after researchers accounted for whether participants lived in cities or rural villages. The findings suggest that social and environmental surroundings play a much larger role in shaping women’s sexual lives than subtle variations in facial structure.

No human face is an exact mirror image from left to right. Biologists refer to small, random differences between the left and right sides of the face or body as fluctuating asymmetry, a trait that takes shape mainly before birth and during childhood growth. Because illness, poor nutrition, maternal stress, or difficult living conditions can disrupt balanced two-sided growth, evolutionary researchers have proposed that greater symmetry may act as an outward sign of developmental resilience and physical health, although recent reviews indicate that links between facial symmetry and actual medical health are weak and inconsistent.

That evolutionary framework prompted psychologists to test whether physical symmetry shapes human mating behavior, beginning with an influential 1994 study that found people with more symmetrical bodies reported having more lifetime sexual partners. Later…
items.t: Evolutionary hypothesis linking facial symmetry to women’s mating behavior fails to hold up in new study

items.title: People with ADHD have higher odds of a wide range of gut symptoms, study finds
items.summary:
A meta-analysis of 23 studies found that people with ADHD had 48% higher odds of experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms than people without ADHD. The odds were also elevated for specific symptoms, including irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, and encopresis, the repeated involuntary passing of stool. The paper was published in the Journal of Attention Disorders .

Neurodivergence refers to differences in brain functioning and behavior from what is considered typical. It encompasses conditions such as dyslexia, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ADHD is estimated to affect about 5% of children and 3% to 4% of adults.

Although both genetic and environmental factors appear to contribute to these conditions, their exact causes remain incompletely understood. Recent research has increasingly focused on the gut-brain axis, the communication system connecting the gastrointestinal tract and the brain. Studies have found that people with ASD, OCD, and ADHD tend to have somewhat different compositions of gut microorganisms than people without these conditions.

Researchers have proposed that imbalances in gut microorganisms may activate the gut’s immune system and produce low-grade inflammation, contributing to gastrointestinal problems. Consistent with this possibility, people with ASD are more likely to experience gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, and people with OCD show high rates of bowel disorders.

items.t: People with ADHD have higher odds of a wide range of gut symptoms, study finds

items.title: Psychologists find a hidden asymmetry in how people judge potential partners
items.summary:
When people think about what they want in a romantic partner, they tend to name more positive qualities than negative ones, yet they agree far less on which flaws to avoid. New research published in European Journal of Social Psychology suggests that desirable partner traits cluster tightly around a shared ideal, whereas undesirable traits span a much wider range of meanings. Because people vary so much in the flaws they reject, negative traits turned out to be much more informative than positive ones for predicting hypothetical online dating decisions.

Online dating platforms require users to form quick impressions of strangers from brief text descriptions and a handful of photos. Most psychological research on partner preferences has focused on the specific meaning, or content, of the personality traits people seek, identifying widely desired qualities such as warmth, kindness, intelligence, and trustworthiness. Rather than looking only at what individual traits mean, psychologists can also examine their broader structural patterns, specifically how frequently positive and negative traits come to mind and how closely traits of the same type resemble one another.

Work in social cognition indicates that good and bad traits are not simple mirror images of each other. For instance, a 2012 study of person descriptions found that adults naturally used a much wider variety of words when describing people they disliked than when describing people they liked. Building on similar patterns across language and memory, researchers introduced the Evaluative Information Ecology model…
items.t: Psychologists find a hidden asymmetry in how people judge potential partners

items.title: Criticism from Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan cut Trump’s sway over Republicans in half in experiment on the Epstein files
items.summary:
Republican voters tend to follow Donald Trump’s lead even when he takes an unpopular stance, yet new experimental research published in Public Opinion Quarterly indicates that his influence has limits. Examining the controversy over releasing government records tied to Jeffrey Epstein, the study found that pushback from Democratic lawmakers failed to dent Trump’s sway, whereas counterarguments from conservative media personalities Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan cut his influence on policy attitudes and lowered his approval ratings. The findings suggest that apparent blind loyalty to a dominant political leader may stem less from an unbreakable cult of personality than from a shortage of trusted opposition within the leader’s own ideological camp.

Democratic government rests on political accountability, the idea that citizens monitor what elected officials do and withdraw support when leaders act against public wishes. In practice, public opinion research frequently documents the opposite pattern, known as opinion leadership, in which partisans adjust their own policy preferences to match whatever stance their favored politicians announce. For instance, a 2015 field experiment with U.S. state legislators and their constituents found that when lawmakers sent letters staking out policy positions that conflicted with voters’ earlier views, constituents tended to adopt the legislators’ positions rather than rate those officials more negatively.

No modern political figure has prompted more debate over partisan cue-following than Donald Trump. In a 2018 survey experiment with…
items.t: Criticism from Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan cut Trump’s sway over Republicans in half in experiment on the Epstein files

items.title: Psychiatrists reveal unusual case in which 71-year-old farmer asked to be tied with ropes to calm his severe anxiety
items.summary:
A recent medical case report describes an unusual behavior in an older man who repeatedly asked his relatives to tie him to his bed with ropes during episodes of overwhelming inner restlessness. Published in The Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders , the report suggests that severe anxiety in late life can sometimes manifest through unexpected physical actions rather than classic emotional complaints. Recognizing these atypical signs may help doctors start appropriate treatment and avoid mistaking treatable anxiety for psychotic or neurological illnesses.

Generalized anxiety disorder involves chronic, hard-to-control worry about everyday life, and it can occur alongside panic attacks, which are sudden surges of intense fear and physical tension. While younger adults tend to describe feeling nervous or fearful, older adults frequently express anxiety through somatic symptoms, meaning emotional distress shows up primarily as physical bodily complaints or persistent health worries.

When an elderly patient displays intense agitation and unusual behaviors, clinicians can easily confuse anxiety with other serious conditions. Doctors must consider psychosis, which involves a loss of contact with reality such as delusions or hallucinations, as well as delirium, a sudden state of mental confusion often triggered by physical illness. Unusual late-life behaviors can also resemble neurocognitive disorders like dementia, which cause progressive declines in memory and thinking.

Clinicians also look for akathisia, an agonizing feeling of inner restlessness and an inability to…
items.t: Psychiatrists reveal unusual case in which 71-year-old farmer asked to be tied with ropes to calm his severe anxiety

items.title: Antagonistic and impulsive traits are linked to cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing on Instagram
items.summary:
A survey of Iranian university students found that those with more pronounced Antagonism and Disinhibition, two maladaptive personality traits, were more likely to report harmful online behaviors such as cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing. In contrast, students higher in Anankastia, a trait marked by perfectionism and rigid rule-following, were less likely to report several of these behaviors. The paper was published in BMC Psychology .

Social media has become an important part of everyday life. It allows people to communicate, maintain relationships, and connect with communities around the world. However, these platforms can also facilitate harmful behaviors, including cyberbullying, cyberstalking, online fraud, trolling, and various other forms of online aggression. Such behaviors can have serious consequences for victims, including financial losses, emotional distress, anxiety, and depression.

Researchers have increasingly investigated whether personality traits are associated with people’s likelihood of engaging in harmful online behaviors. Previous studies have found that individuals who are less agreeable, less conscientious, and more emotionally unstable tend to report higher levels of various antisocial online behaviors. However, most research has focused on normal personality traits, while relatively little is known about the relationships between harmful online behaviors and maladaptive personality traits, which represent more extreme and potentially dysfunctional patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving.

items.t: Antagonistic and impulsive traits are linked to cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing on Instagram

items.title: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth
items.summary:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth. 

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020 . What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017 .

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens , a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to…
items.t: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

items.title: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents
items.summary:
It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the new baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge. 

Emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s important to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

items.t: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents
